title: Rate of Reaction
seo_title: SSS 3 Chemistry: Rate of Reaction Worksheets (WAEC/NECO)
standard_text: Reaction rate as the change in concentration (or mass, or volume) per unit time; factors that affect the rate: nature of reactants, concentration (pressure), surface area, temperature and catalysts; collision theory; the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution; measuring rates of reaction. (summary of the senior secondary Chemistry curriculum, SSS 3; WAEC and NECO syllabuses)
meta_desc: Free SSS 3 Chemistry worksheets (senior secondary curriculum, WAEC and NECO): collision theory, factors that affect rate, measuring rates of reaction, collision theory and catalysts and rate data and investigations. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Only collisions with enough energy and the right orientation are effective.
body_html:
How to think about it

Collision theory: particles must collide with enough energy (at least the activation energy) and with the correct orientation for a reaction to happen. The rate increases if collisions happen more often or more of them are effective.

Higher concentration or pressure and larger surface area give more collisions per second. A higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy, so more of them have enough energy to react (seen on a Maxwell–Boltzmann curve). A catalyst gives a pathway with a lower activation energy. Rates are measured by gas volume, mass loss or colour change.

Example

50 cm³ of gas forms in 25 s. Average rate?

volume ÷ time

Answer: 2 cm³·s⁻¹

Example

Why does powdered zinc react faster than a lump?

Surface area

Answer: it has a larger surface area, so there are more collisions

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a catalyst increases the energy of the particles.
  • Thinking a higher temperature only increases the number of collisions.
  • Thinking a catalyst changes the yield.
